source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-001 - Window opening control devices (WOCD)
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: To provide an alternative solution in meeting the requirements of Sentences 9.8.8.1 (4) and (5) …

description: We build houses and small residential buildings in Alberta. Many of our bedroom windows sit low to the floor with a long drop outside, so they need a way to stop small children from opening them wide. We want to fit window opening control devices that limit the sash to a narrow opening of about 100 mm. The same bedroom windows also have to work as emergency escape windows that open from the inside without keys, tools or special knowledge. We would like to use devices that meet the ASTM F2090 fall-prevention standard, which have an emergency release. We understand these devices are not allowed in adaptable or barrier-free dwelling units. What are we varying, and what would the building officer expect?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'openable windows in buildings of residential occupancy shall be protected by'

mapping.codedb_title: Egress Windows or Doors for Bedrooms
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'openable from the inside without the use of keys, tools or special knowledge'

notes: Condition: WOCD mechanisms are not permitted in adaptable or barrier-free dwelling units. Province-wide variance. Edmonton Policy B23-02 (2024-12) restates the same variance and is not a separate case. No Division A/C articles cited.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-003 - Insulation below a heated floor
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: This province-wide variance will allow an alternative solution to the provisions under Section 9.36. for …

description: I am building a house in Alberta with in-floor hydronic heating tubes in the basement slab. The energy provisions call for a thick layer of rigid insulation under any heated floor that sits on the ground, and that amount makes radiant floor heating hard to justify. I want to install a thinner under-slab insulation layer, roughly half of what the table asks for, while still meeting the energy requirements for the walls, roof and windows. The slab is in contact with the ground, either below or above the frost line. Which requirement am I varying, and what do I need to show the building officer?

mapping.as_cited: Sentence 9.36.2.8.(1) and Tables 9.36.2.8.-A and B, NBC(AE) 2023
mapping.codedb_title: Thermal Characteristics of Building Assemblies Below-Grade or in Contact with the Ground
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'the effective thermal resistance of building assemblies that are below-grade or in contact with the ground'

notes: Variance allows a minimum RSI 1.32 (R 7.5) under-slab insulation for heated floors in ground contact, instead of RSI 2.32 to 2.84 in the tables. Objective and functional attribution cited: OE1.1 and F92. Applies to Part 9 buildings with a heating system creating a heated floor in contact with the ground.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-004 - Sprinkler-protected glazing in fire-resistant wall assemblies
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: glazing assemblies are permitted to be installed for interior or exterior fire rated assemblies required …

description: We are designing a building where the owner wants large clear glass panels in a fire-rated corridor wall, in the enclosure of an exit stair and in an exterior wall, so people can see through instead of looking at wired glass or glass block. We would protect the glass with listed window sprinkler heads on an automatic sprinkler system. The glazing has not been through the standard fire endurance test for rated walls, because that test does not address sprinkler-protected glass. It has been evaluated to the sprinkler-protected window test standard instead. Can we use it in rated assemblies, and which conditions apply?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'shall be determined on the basis of the results of tests conducted in conformance with CAN/ULC-S101'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Where a fire-resistance rating or a fire-protection rating is required in this Section'

notes: Conditions include SCC-accredited evaluation to CAN/ULC-S136, specific-application window sprinklers, fixed heat-strengthened/tempered/ceramic glass, not in a firewall, not in required exits of high buildings or residential/care/treatment occupancies; fire alarm required. Context articles (fire alarm and sprinkler design) are cited in the variance text but are not provisions varied.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-005 - Occupancy classification of oil and gas processing buildings
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Oil or gas processing buildings may be classified as Group F, Division 2 medium-hazard occupancy …

description: We operate small, portable oil and gas production facilities outside urban areas: compressor stations, heater, pump and separator packages, treaters and similar equipment housed in buildings of about 150 square metres or less that people only enter occasionally. By default these buildings would be treated as high-hazard industrial occupancies, which brings tougher requirements, including more egress doorways. We want them classified as medium-hazard instead, backed by a risk assessment from an Alberta-licensed engineer covering ventilation, gas detection, emergency shutdown and fire detection, plus industry safety guidelines. Larger buildings would get two remote exit doors with panic hardware. Which code provisions are we departing from?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'a minimum of 2 egress doorways located so that one doorway could provide egress'

notes: The only Division B provision in the Code References is Clause 3.3.1.5.(1)(c) with Table 3.3.1.5.-A (two egress doorways for rooms over the table limits in floor areas not sprinklered throughout). Division A defined terms for high-hazard/medium-hazard industrial occupancy apply but are not Division B. Spatial-separation conditions cite whole Subsections (not articles) so they are not in gold or context.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-007 - Maximum span values for joists, rafters and beams
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: The values for the maximum spans of joists, rafters, and beams referenced in Article 9.23.4.2. …

description: We frame houses and small buildings in Alberta and want to size floor joists, rafters and beams using The Span Book, the 2020 edition published by the Canadian Wood Council. It covers many alternative configurations that the span tables printed in the code do not. The Span Book tables are produced by the same organization that generates the code's own span tables, but they have not gone through the formal code committee review. Can we take maximum spans from The Span Book for our permit drawings, and which code requirement are we departing from?

mapping.codedb_title: Spans for Joists, Rafters and Beams
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'spans for wood joists and rafters shall conform to the spans shown in Span Tables'

notes: Province-wide variance recognising the 2020 Span Book values for Part 9 wood framing. Appendix Note A-9.23.4.2. is cited by the source. No Division A/C articles.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-008(REV1) - Residential exhaust outlet clearance from air intakes
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Provides an alternative solution to Sentence 9.32.3.13.(4) for the minimum clearance requirement for domestic exhaust …

description: In our house design the clothes dryer, bathroom fan and kitchen exhaust outlets end up close to the fresh-air intake for the heat recovery ventilator. They are closer than the 1.8 m the code asks for between a moist-air exhaust outlet and an air intake. Each outlet sits at the same level as, or higher than, the intake. The house is a single dwelling or a house with a secondary suite. We want to use the reduced clearance of about 900 mm shown in the province's clearance diagram for these cases. Which ventilation provision are we varying?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'exhaust outlets that discharge air containing moisture, such as bathroom ventilation and clothes dryer exhaust outlets'

notes: The reduction (1 800 mm to 900 mm) applies only where the moist-air outlet is horizontal to or above the intake; manufacturer instructions that are more stringent still govern. Applies to an individual dwelling unit or a house with a secondary suite. The superseded 23-BCV-008 (2024-06) is the same topic and not a separate case.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-009 - CSA B52:23 Mechanical refrigeration code
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Conformance with CSA B52:23, “Mechanical refrigeration code,” is considered to comply with the installation standard …

description: We install heat pumps and air-conditioning equipment. New units on the market use the lower-impact A2L refrigerants, and those units are designed to the 2023 edition of the mechanical refrigeration code. The building code, however, designates the 2018 edition of that standard for installing refrigeration equipment, including the mounting, clearances and air supply. We want the building officer to accept installations done to the 2023 edition so we can use the new refrigerants. Which installation requirements are we varying, in houses and in larger buildings?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'the installation of heating and air-conditioning equipment, including mechanical refrigeration equipment'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'the installation of heating and air-conditioning equipment, including mechanical refrigeration equipment'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'they shall be the editions designated in Table 1.3.1.2.'

notes: The Application statement names 6.2.1.5.(1) and 9.33.5.2.(1); Table 1.3.1.2. (applicable editions, here CSA B52:18) is the reason the newer edition needs a variance, so 1.3.1.2. is kept as context.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-010R1 - Engineer's authentication for welding procedures
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: To provide an alternative solution to the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) …

description: We fabricate steel skids for mounting mechanical equipment and some proprietary structural components at a shop outside Canada. Structural steel must follow the Canadian steel design standard, which in turn expects fabricators to be certified by the Canadian Welding Bureau. Our shop is not certified to that standard, and our welding follows the American structural welding code. We would rely on an Alberta registered engineer to authenticate the documentation, confirm the welding procedures and fabricator competence, and have the owner's inspector verify welder qualifications in the shop. Can this be accepted instead of company certification?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'made of structural steel shall conform to CSA S16'

notes: The CWB-certification requirement reaches Division B through CSA S16 (Clause 24.3) referenced from 4.3.4.1.(1); Division C 2.2.2.4.(1) (owner evidence of CWB certification) and Division A 1.4.1.2. are also cited but are not Division B. Supersedes 23-BCV-010 (2025-02).

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-011R1 - Polyethylene film for greenhouse enclosures
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Polyethylene film used to enclose commercial greenhouse facilities is not required to conform to CAN/ULC-S109, …

description: We run a commercial greenhouse and want to cover it with polyethylene film made for plant growing. These greenhouse films carry additives that help plants but they generally do not meet the flame test standard written for tents and air-supported structures, and the treatments needed to meet it cut the ultraviolet light plants need. Part of our one-storey greenhouse would be open to customers who buy plants. We would keep public aisles wide with exits in two directions, make the exit doors wider than normal, use a lower floor area per person for the occupant load, post exit signs and prepare a fire safety plan. Which provision are we varying?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'all tarpaulins and decorative materials used in connection with these structures'

notes: Option 1: staff-only plant-growing greenhouse, film flame spread rating not above 25. Option 2: one-storey Group F, Division 3 greenhouse with limited public retail access plus aisle, door-width (+40%), 4.6 m2/person occupant load, exit signage and fire safety plan conditions. Earlier versions (14-BCV-009 ABC 2014, 19-BCV-011 NBC 2019, 23-BCV-011 2025-02) are the same topic; the newest is used.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-012R1 - Permanent wood foundations with mechanically laminated timber panels for Part 9 residential buildings
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: MLTP are not included within the scope of the CSA S406-16 standard. Therefore, permanent wood …

description: We want to build permanent wood foundations for houses using mechanically laminated timber panels instead of conventional preserved-wood framing. These panels are outside the scope of the standard that the code accepts for permanent wood foundations, so the only route would be a full structural design under the engineering part of the code, with a registered professional doing field reviews. A University of Alberta guide gives pre-engineered structural designs for these panel foundations on residential buildings. Can we follow that guide, and what must the permit drawings show?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Foundations of wood-frame construction shall conform to'

notes: Application: Group C residential occupancies designed under Part 9. Condition: project-specific MLTP details must appear on the permit drawings; panels outside the guide scope must use the engineered route. Division C 2.4.1.2.(1)-(2) (registered professional design and field review) is cited but not Division B.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-013 / 19-EDB-002 - Elevator and passenger-elevating devices
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator) and Provincial Administrator Elevating Devices
source.excerpt: Where a passenger elevator is used instead of a lift conforming to CSA B355, or …

description: We are designing a small building where barrier-free access to one level could be provided by a platform lift or a limited-use limited-application elevator. The owner would rather install a regular passenger elevator. A regular elevator car normally has to be long enough for a patient stretcher, which a lift or limited-use elevator is exempt from. Our vertical travel is under 7.6 m and the car would meet the minimum clear floor size set for barrier-free passenger lifts. We also assume firefighters' emergency operation would not be needed, as it is not required for lifts. Can the stretcher-size rule be set aside here?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'adequate access for a patient stretcher'

notes: Conditions: vertical travel 7 620 mm or less; car not smaller than the minimum in 3.8.3.7.(2); applicants give the AHJ a copy of the building permit and elevating devices permit. The elevating-device code aspects (ASME A17.1/CSA B44, CSA B355) are outside the NBC; the NBC provision varied is the stretcher-size requirement. Earlier versions 14-BCV-006 and 19-BCV-003 are the same topic.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-014 - Multi-level storage racking systems
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Multi-level storage racking systems are permitted to be classified as special and unusual structures according …

description: We are planning a distribution facility with a multi-level storage racking system: self-supporting steel racks with intermediate walkway levels so staff can reach stored goods without ladders. Some safety codes officers treat each access level as a storey, a mezzanine or an interconnected floor space. Only authorized staff would enter, with low occupant loads. We want the racking assessed as a special and unusual structure designed to good fire protection engineering practice, with a fire safety plan, sprinklers under every platform, a fire alarm, emergency power, guards and toe-boards, and two remote egress stairs from each level. Which provision are we relying on?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'shall be protected against fire spread and collapse in conformance with good fire protection engineering practice'

notes: Permitted in medium/low-hazard industrial or mercantile buildings; not required to meet Subsection 3.2.6. (high buildings) or Section 3.8. (conditions 1.5). Other conditions cite the National Fire Code and whole Subsections 3.2.4. and 3.2.7. (not articles). Article 3.3.1.18. (guards) is the only other Division B article cited. Earlier versions 14-BCV-015 and 19-BCV-008 are the same topic.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-017 - Unvented roof assembly
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Sentence 9.19.1.1.(1) suggests there are some types of roof assemblies where venting is not necessary, …

description: We build houses and small residential buildings and want to use unvented roof assemblies, where there is no ventilated space between the insulation and the roof sheathing. The code expects that space to be vented so moisture can escape unless it can be shown that venting is unnecessary, and the only examples it gives are specialized factory-built roofs and the lower portion of mansard or gambrel roofs. We want to follow the design requirements in an Alberta-specific building science evaluation report on unvented roofs and attach the report to the permit application. Which provisions are we varying?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Except where it can be shown to be unnecessary'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'The lower portion of a mansard or gambrel style roof need not be ventilated'

notes: Application: roof assemblies in Part 9 residential buildings; the evaluation report must accompany the permit application. The 2019 version (19-BCV-022, 2022-04) is the same topic. Note A-9.19.1.1.(1) is cited by the source.

source.title: STANDATA variance 23-BCV-018 - Vented soffit protection
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Sentences 9.10.14.5.(12), 9.10.15.5.(11) and 9.10.12.4.(2) and (3) of the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta …

description: We build houses close to the property line. Where the roof soffit sits within 1.2 m of the lot line, or a floor projection covers the wall between two suites, the code wants a closed soffit covered in sheet steel, unvented aluminum, gypsum board, plywood, OSB or lumber. That forces us to add roof surface vents instead of venting through the soffit. We want to use a material with an intumescent coating on a vented fibreglass or metal base, which seals its openings in a fire, fastened under the projection with a vented finish soffit over it. It has been tested at an accredited lab to perform at least as well as 11 mm plywood. Which provisions are we varying?

mapping.codedb_title: Construction of Exposing Building Face and Walls above Exposing Building Face
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'they shall a) have no openings'

mapping.codedb_title: Construction of Exposing Building Face of Houses
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'they shall a) have no openings'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'shall have no unprotected openings and shall be protected in accordance with Sentence (3)'

notes: Conditions: lab test accredited by the Standards Council of Canada showing performance at least equal to 11 mm plywood (radiant heat flux 50 kW/m2, Appendix A Table 1) and installation per manufacturer instructions or test documentation. Earlier version 19-BCV-017 (2020-11) is the same topic.

source.title: STANDATA variance 14-BCV-002R1 - Tall wall generic engineered details
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Table 9.23.10.1. specifies the requirements for exterior walls only up to 3.6 metres and for …

description: We build houses and want some walls taller than the stud tables allow, more than 3.6 m for exterior walls or 4.2 m for interior walls. Walls above those heights have to be individually engineered, which adds cost and time to every house. We would like to use a published residential tall wall guideline, prepared by an engineering firm and distributed by the home builders' association, in place of project-specific engineering. The tall wall details for the project would be shown on the drawings submitted for the building permit. Walls outside the guideline's criteria would still be engineered. Which code provision are we varying?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'The size and spacing of studs shall conform to Table 9.23.10.1.'

notes: Archived 2014-edition variance (no 2019 or 2023 equivalent found), kept because the Part 9 rule it varies is unchanged in 2023 (stud size and spacing table). The table values were not re-checked (tables are not in the code database).

source.title: STANDATA variance 14-BCV-003R1 - Wind data for low-rise buildings guideline
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Article 9.7.4.3. of the Alberta Building Code 2014 (ABC 2014) requires that performance grades for …

description: We design and build houses across Alberta. The code makes us choose performance grades for windows, doors and skylights using a Canadian supplement. Its simplified method for wind load and driving rain pressure uses exposure factors intended for high-rise buildings, so the ratings it gives for low houses are far higher than the actual weather loads require. We want to take the design values from a guideline that a registered engineering firm prepared for low-rise residential buildings and that the home builders' association publishes, instead of paying for project-specific engineering. Which provision are we varying?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Performance grades for windows, doors and skylights shall be selected according to the Canadian Supplement'

notes: Archived 2014-edition variance; the guideline is tied to Part 9 of ABC 2014 and the wording of the article is unchanged in the 2023 text, but the guideline itself may not be current. Kept as a Part 9 building-envelope example.

source.title: STANDATA variance 14-BCV-008 - Separation of suites in strip malls
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: In a strip mall, suites of business and personal services occupancy and suites of mercantile …

description: We are developing a one-storey strip mall with sprinklers and a fire alarm system. Each suite opens straight to the outside with at least two exits, so there is no enclosed public corridor. Dentist and lawyer type office suites will sit next to retail shops. The code lets sprinklered buildings skip the fire separation between those two kinds of suites when they are served by a wide public corridor, but a strip mall has no such corridor, so as written we would need rated separations between every suite. We want the same exception to apply to our strip mall. Which provisions are we varying?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Occupancies that are served by public corridors conforming to Clause 3.3.1.4.(4)(b) in a building that is sprinklered throughout'

renumbered successor with matching title and text (ABC 2014 9.10.9.13. is now Separation of Suites): 2023 text says 'In sprinklered buildings, suites of business and personal services occupancy and mercantile occupancy'

notes: Trap: in the 2023 edition 9.10.9.13. is "Separation of Residential Occupancies"; the ABC 2014 suite-separation article is now 9.10.9.15. (both sentences matched by text). Conditions: one storey, sprinklered, fire alarm, two exits per suite directly outside, no residential or institutional occupancy; assembly suite separated per the major-occupancy table. Archived 2014 variance; the Part 3 and Part 9 provisions it varies still need a corridor to qualify for the exception.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 23-BCI-017 - Photoluminescent exit signs
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: The charging light source provided for PL exit signs do not require connection to the …

description: We are installing listed photoluminescent exit signs in a building. These signs need a light source that stays on to keep them charged, and we have been told the circuit serving exit sign lighting must serve only emergency equipment and be connected to the emergency power supply. Our charging lights would be on a separate circuit used for nothing else, with no automatic timers, with controls reachable only by authorized staff, using lamps that match the sign listing, and installed to the manufacturer's listed instructions. Can the charging lights stay off emergency power, whether the project is a larger building or a small residential building?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'shall a) serve no equipment other than emergency equipment'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'shall a) serve no equipment other than emergency equipment'

notes: Interpretation, not a variance. It applies to both the Part 3 article and its Part 9 twin. The NECB (lighting power exemptions for exit signs) is cited but is a different code.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 25-GCI-003/23-BCI-020 - Mechanically vented appliances
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator) and Provincial Gas Administrator
source.excerpt: Category I and II appliances do not meet the definition of either mechanically vented or …

description: We are installing new gas furnaces and water heaters in houses. Some safety codes officers say that any appliance where room air can mix with the combustion products is at risk of spilling exhaust when the house is depressurized, so a make-up air supply would be required. Our equipment is fan-powered and vents through a sealed pipe to the outdoors, and some units draw their combustion air directly from outside. Which kinds of fuel-fired heating and water-heating appliances count as mechanically vented or direct-vented, so the dwelling unit does not need protection against depressurization?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'other than direct-vented or mechanically vented types'

notes: Interpretation applies to Part 9 buildings. Category I and II appliances are not mechanically vented; Category III and IV count as mechanically vented; direct-vent appliances with enclosed passageways to the exterior count as direct-vented. Division A defined terms and CSA B149.1 are cited but are not Division B.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 23-BCI-034 - Elevator operation and accessibility for residential buildings
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: The authority for ordering an owner to make an elevator operational is under Article 3.8.2.3. …

description: I live in a residential building that is required to have a barrier-free path of travel, and the only passenger elevator has been out of service for months. Residents who use wheelchairs or have limited mobility cannot get to or from their homes. The building rules only require an elevator to be available for firefighters in high buildings, and the elevator code does not oblige an owner to keep a lift running. Which provision of the building code lets a safety codes officer order the owner to get the elevator working again?

mapping.codedb_title: Areas Requiring a Barrier-Free Path of Travel
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'a barrier-free path of travel from the entrances required by Sentence 3.8.2.2.(1) to be barrier-free shall be provided'
same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Where passenger elevators are used in a barrier-free path of travel'

notes: Interpretation. Article 3.8.3.7. (passenger-elevating devices in a barrier-free path) is listed in the source's Code References and defines the devices the interpretation covers. Article 3.8.2.1. (exceptions: houses, townhouses etc. are exempt) is discussed in the source and kept as context. Division A 1.4.2.1. (barrier-free definition) is cited but is not Division B.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 23-BCI-022 - Energy efficiency exemptions for buildings
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Sentence 9.36.1.3.(7) of the NBC(AE) provides for exemptions where the building is not required to …

description: We are putting up small industrial buildings at an oil and gas site to shelter compressors, pumps, heaters, separators, electrical gear and similar equipment. Nobody works inside them day to day. There are no offices or washrooms, and workers only enter for short maintenance or servicing tasks. We also plan some tent and membrane-supported structures. We want to confirm that the energy efficiency requirements for small buildings, and the national energy code for larger ones, do not have to be applied to these buildings, and what information the building officer will want to see.

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'are not required to be conditioned spaces are exempted from the requirements of this Section'

notes: The sentence cross-refers to Article 9.25.2.1. (garage insulation), kept as context. NECB Division C 2.2.1.1.(2) (AHJ may exempt where occupancy is impractical to apply) is cited but is a different code.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 23-BCI-035 - Attached garage separation serving a house with a secondary suite
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator)
source.excerpt: Sentence 9.10.9.18.(3) of the NBC(AE) waives the requirement for a one-hour fire separation between an …

description: We are building a house with a basement secondary suite and an attached garage. The code waives the one-hour fire separation between an attached garage and the house when the garage serves only the dwelling unit it is attached to. Because a house with a secondary suite contains two dwelling units, we are not sure the waiver can be used. We want to rely on it, finishing the garage interior as required and installing an air barrier between the garage and the living space so fumes cannot pass through. May we leave out the fire separation between the garage and the house?

mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'Where a storage garage serves only the dwelling unit to which it is attached or in which it is built'

notes: Interpretation, not a variance: the source says the waiver is intended to apply to a house with a secondary suite, while the air barrier requirement in the same article and the garage interior finish still apply. Context articles are the other house-with-secondary-suite provisions the source cites for comparison.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 23-BCI-042 / 20-PCB-011R1 - Hydronic heating systems
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator) and Provincial Plumbing Administrator
source.excerpt: Proper verification of compliance with Sentence 9.33.4.1.(1) for hydronic heating systems in buildings not within …

description: We design and install in-floor radiant, baseboard and radiator hydronic heating in houses where the code does not require professionals on the building design. The code says heating systems must follow good practice such as the listed industry manuals, but it does not say how a building officer can verify that a hydronic design does. We would submit either a pre-engineered package prepared by an Alberta engineer, with project-specific design by an engineer or a certified hydronics designer, or a custom design by those same people. Will that be accepted as showing the hydronic system meets the design requirement?

mapping.codedb_title: Design of Heating and Air-conditioning Systems
mapping.verification: same number, same requirement: 2023 text says 'shall be designed, constructed and installed to conform with good practice'

notes: Interpretation applies to hydronic systems heating the building interior (not exterior snowmelt or pool heaters). Division C 2.4.1.1.(3) (full professional involvement) is cited but is not Division B.

source.title: STANDATA interpretation 23-BCI-016R1 - Barrier-free design requirements: relaxations
source.issuer: Government of Alberta (Municipal Affairs, Provincial Building Administrator) and Provincial Barrier-Free Administrator
source.excerpt: Sentence 3.8.2.1.(1) of the NBC(AE) allows the AHJ or SCO the discretion to assess building …

description: We plan to open a micro-brewery with a tasting room in a multi-tenant building in Calgary. The code has no brewery-specific rules, and the city says a micro-brewery would not be high hazard but could be treated as medium or low hazard industrial. If the tasting room stays under about a tenth of the building area it can be treated as part of the brewery with no fire separation between them, but a larger tasting room is treated as its own major occupancy. We also need to know how to separate the brewery from the neighbouring tenants and what an architect or engineer must prepare if our design departs from the prescriptive rules.
